title: How often should you change programs?
summary: NH's short answer is: change programs only when you stop progressing. He says novices should stay on one program longer than usual and modify it, intermediates should try programs while taking notes so they can write their own, and advanced lifters keep one template for life and only swap lifts within movement patterns.
claims: Understanding programming is the true path for naturals; once you do, limits stop existing
Mindset and effort matter more than the program, especially for novices: a park trainee who goes hard on chin-ups and push-ups will outgain someone with a perfect program who doesn't put in the work
Follow a program exactly; the 20% you remove might be what holds the other 80% together
Valid reasons to change programs: you can't progress, it lacks set/rep manipulation to push volume, or its exercise selection no longer works
When a program you chose fails, reflect on why you chose it so the next choice doesn't repeat the mistake
Most novice programs are too short (around four weeks) and try to make you strong too fast; spend about double the usual time on them
The novice phase builds the base, which should be as wide as possible; thanks to muscle memory you'll never be that weak again, so enjoy it
Modify your novice program freely, even suboptimally, to learn programming on a template that has already proven to work
Intermediates know what they want; stick with a program as long as possible unless your goals change radically
While following intermediate programs, take notes on the movements, frequency and exercises you like, dislike, or that help you rehab, to map your body and eventually write your own program
5/3/1 is an idea, an application of volume and intensity, rather than a program
A program is a tool, not a religion; if it stops producing progress or gets you injured after you've done everything right, move on
The perfect program, flexible enough that you never need to change it, is one only you can write
Gifted lifters can progress for years on minimalist programs, so don't copy people more gifted than you; average lifters need flexibility and to understand the variables early
He wrote his current program as an intermediate and has run it for close to two years with good progress
If a program still makes you progress, never change it; switching out of boredom points to a high-change personality
Advanced lifters keep the same template for life and only swap lifts within the fixed movement patterns
Change programs as little as possible, but never at the cost of progression
